h: Three centuries of gardening in one walk
p: What makes Wrest Park so satisfying is that you can read garden history in the ground as you walk. The formal canals and straight avenues near the centre come from the early 1700s, when gardens were all about order and showing off. Later, Lancelot 'Capability' Brown was brought in and softened the edges with more natural-looking woodland and winding water, and there's a monument to him in the grounds. Then the Victorians added their own flourishes near the house. It's like walking through a timeline laid out in hedges, lawns and statues.

The house itself is younger than many people assume. It was built in the 1830s for Thomas de Grey, 2nd Earl de Grey, who was a keen amateur architect and drew heavily on French styles, which is why it feels so different from the usual English country pile. Look out for the elegant orangery beside the formal gardens, a lovely spot when the light's coming through the glass.

The estate's story didn't stop with the de Greys. During the First World War the house served as a hospital for wounded soldiers, and later the site was used for agricultural research for decades, so there's more to discover than just aristocrats and their hobbies.

Plan on at least half a day. The paths are long and mostly level, which suits pushchairs and gentle walkers, though some woodland routes get muddy after rain. Silsoe village is on the doorstep, and if you're making a weekend of it, the vintage aircraft of the Shuttleworth Collection at Old Warden are within an easy drive.
